content: An intervention is recommended if it is likely to reduce health inequities among infants, mothers, and their families, particularly in vulnerable or disadvantaged groups. During the meeting, each recommendation was supported by a rationale, implementation considerations, and research priorities. The chairpersons for the consultation meetings held in April and November 2016 were Dr. Maria Elena del Socorro Jefferds, Dr. Rukhsana Haider, Ms. Solange Durão, and Dr. Susan Jack, nominated by the WHO Secretariat and approved by the guideline development group. Consensus decision-making procedures were established at the start of the meetings, including rules for agreement and documentation. At least two-thirds of the group needed to be present for initial discussions on evidence and proposed recommendations. Members voted on recommendations via a secret ballot using an online form, with abstentions not permitted. If unanimous consensus was not achieved, further deliberations and a second round of voting were conducted. If consensus was still not reached, a two-thirds majority vote was required for approval. Voting records will be retained by WHO for up to five years. The first draft of the guideline was prepared by the responsible technical officer with input from the steering group. Technical editing and proofreading were completed by a contracted party. Sixteen of the 21 invited peer reviewers agreed to participate, and their feedback was reviewed by the steering group to refine the document while maintaining consistency with the original intent. The guideline on protecting, promoting, and supporting breastfeeding in maternity and newborn care facilities will be disseminated through the WHO website, including the WHO Nutrition website and the e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions (eLENA). It will also be shared with international partners, WHO country and regional offices, health ministries, collaborating centers, universities, other UN agencies, and NGOs. An implementation guide, incorporating the recommendations, the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes, and the Baby-friendly Hospital Initiative, has been developed by WHO and UNICEF and will be published separately. The WHO steering group will monitor research developments related to breastfeeding in maternity and newborn care facilities, particularly in areas where evidence quality is low. If an update is warranted or concerns arise about the guideline's validity, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development will coordinate the update following WHO's formal guideline development procedures. As the guideline approaches its 10-year review period, the Department, in collaboration with internal partners, will conduct a search for new evidence to determine the need for revisions.
